evaluation.positioning_hook: A washed-up jazz pianist in Lisbon has days to finish a song for a bunker kingpin before an asteroid hits, but falling for a woman who refuses to be bought turns salvation into a moral trap.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The asteroid countdown, bunker scarcity, and doomed romance give the script a clean commercial engine, and the Lisbon hotel setting keeps it visually premium. The audience is real but narrower than a four-quadrant genre play because the movie is built around mood, music, and emotional choice rather than spectacle.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands immediately: a pianist in a collapsing world is being bought for his music while the clock runs out on civilization. The bunker deal, the ticking watch, and the unfinished song all establish the hook early and cleanly.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Morgan is built as a damaged, performative lead with a strong internal contradiction: he wants to survive, but he also wants his art to mean something. Marie, Michel, and George each have distinct energies that make the central triangle feel playable and durable.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a rare blend of apocalyptic romance, jazz performance, and luxury-survival satire without feeling random. The recurring watch motif, the music-as-bargain structure, and the Lisbon hotel micro-world give it a confident authorial stamp.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story has a strong forward engine whenever the bunker deal, the song, or Marie’s choices are in play, and the asteroid countdown keeps pressure on every scene. It does loosen into repeated emotional beats and atmospheric passages, especially in the middle stretch, before the final convergence.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea feels fresh because the apocalypse is filtered through a musician’s bargain, not through action mechanics. The combination of jazz, class anxiety, and end-of-world intimacy lands as immediately legible and unusual.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The hotel functions like a sealed social ecosystem with its own rules, hierarchies, and economies, from the bartender’s barter system to George’s curated bunker culture. Lisbon’s collapse adds texture without overwhelming the chamber-piece scale.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: This has a very specific tonal identity: mournful, romantic, and controlled, with flashes of dread and dark luxury. The script’s voice is unusually consistent in how it treats music, time, and decay, and the repeated ticking motif gives it a signature pulse.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The script keeps revealing that the real subject is not the asteroid but Morgan’s relationship to art, fear, and self-betrayal. George, the bride, the watch, and the bunker all suggest a deeper psychological architecture beneath the surface plot.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Morgan/Marie, Morgan/George, and Morgan/Michel each generate a different kind of scene energy, and the hotel crowd gives the room recurring social pressure. This is not an ensemble in the broad sense, but the supporting web is strong enough to keep the feature alive beyond the lead.

lead_characters.name: Morgan Aireheart
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s, white, American expatriate, professional musician
lead_characters.hook: A gifted but emotionally barricaded jazz pianist living out of a Lisbon hotel, Morgan is running on pride, grief, and denial. He wears composure like armor, but the watch on his wrist and the unfinished song on his desk expose the fracture underneath: he wants to survive the end of the world without becoming the kind of man who can be bought.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a Michael Shannon or Oscar Isaac type role in a prestige feature: a controlled, interior lead who gets to play menace, shame, seduction, and collapse in the same frame. The part offers the rare actorly pleasure of making music, carrying romantic tension, and landing a final moral turn that redefines the character.

lead_characters.name: Marie Freeling
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s, white, American, emotionally guarded, musically literate
lead_characters.hook: Marie is the script’s living counterargument to Morgan’s cynicism: sharp, wounded, funny, and unwilling to confuse survival with surrender. She arrives as a flirtation and becomes the story’s conscience, then its emotional equal, with enough mystery and force to feel like a real life outside the hotel.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the same kind of layered romantic authority as Rooney Mara in Carol or Rebecca Hall in Christine: quiet magnetism, emotional restraint, and a late-breaking moral spine. It also gives a performer the chance to sing, spar, and anchor the film’s emotional release.

lead_characters.name: George
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 60s, affluent, controlled, likely European or international elite
lead_characters.hook: George is the film’s cold-blooded patron saint of preservation, a man who has turned apocalypse into asset management. He speaks in calm, surgical language and never raises his voice, which makes him more dangerous than any overt villain; he is buying culture, buying talent, and buying time.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is prime Christopher Walken / Ralph Fiennes / Michael Stuhlbarg territory: a refined predator who can make every line feel like a velvet threat. The role offers a deliciously controlled performance with intelligence, menace, and a late-film reveal of fear beneath the polish.

lead_characters.name: Michel
lead_characters.hook: Michel is the hotel’s moral ballast, a bartender who understands that civilization is mostly ritual, and that ritual still matters when the sky is falling. He’s dry, observant, and quietly compassionate, with the kind of lived-in dignity that makes him feel like the only adult in the room.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Barkhad Abdi in Captain Phillips or Ben Mendelsohn in Animal Kingdom does so well: make stillness feel loaded and humane. It’s a grounded, scene-stealing supporting part with warmth, wit, and authority.

lead_characters.name: Ava
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s, glamorous, socially agile, emotionally volatile
lead_characters.hook: Ava is the hotel’s opportunist with a pulse, a woman who understands the currency of attention and the desperation of the room better than most. She’s flirtatious, wounded, and harder to read than she first appears, which keeps her from being just another accessory to the men around her.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong supporting territory for an actor who likes playing volatility with wit, in the lane of Jena Malone or Jennifer Jason Leigh in a pressure-cooker ensemble. The role gives a performer sharp entrances, emotional reversals, and a real sense of social intelligence.

lead_characters.name: Markus
lead_characters.hook: Markus is the cautionary mirror of Morgan’s self-destruction: charming enough to be trusted, damaged enough to be dangerous, and weak enough to be manipulated. His presence gives the story its first hard jolt and establishes the moral cost of the bunker economy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play charm curdling into panic, similar to the volatile supporting work in Uncut Gems or The Place Beyond the Pines. It’s a compact but memorable part with real narrative consequence.

lead_characters.name: Nadia
lead_characters.demographics: Female, teen, child/young-adult range, vulnerable, observant
lead_characters.hook: Nadia is the story’s innocence under siege, but she’s not passive; she watches, absorbs, and quietly changes the moral temperature of the room. Her fear gives the apocalypse a human scale, and her presence sharpens the adults’ compromises.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a meaningful young-performer role in the vein of Brooklynn Prince in The Florida Project: emotionally legible, observant, and central to the film’s moral stakes. It gives a young actor a chance to play fear, resilience, and silent witness without being ornamental.

lead_characters.name: Azar
lead_characters.hook: Azar is one of the film’s clearest faces of civilian panic, a father trying to convert valuables into survival for his family. He’s not a plot machine; he’s a pressure point, and his choices make the bunker economy feel brutal and real.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of small but emotionally loaded role that character actors can make unforgettable, in the spirit of Richard Jenkins or John Ortiz in a few scenes. It offers immediate stakes and a lived-in desperation that lands fast.

lead_characters.name: Cyra
lead_characters.hook: Cyra is the exhausted parent trying to keep her family intact while the world’s rules dissolve around her. She’s less a speechmaker than a witness, but her presence gives the family stakes a face and a pulse.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong supporting mother role for an actor who can communicate fear and dignity with minimal dialogue, in the lane of Melissa Leo or Ann Dowd. It’s emotionally specific without needing a huge amount of screen time.

lead_characters.name: Victor Reis
lead_characters.hook: Victor is another version of the world George is curating: cultured, compromised, and already half-owned by the system. He’s a reminder that talent in this movie is always one transaction away from becoming property.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a sleek supporting role for an actor who can play status and unease at once, in the lane of Stanley Tucci or David Strathairn. It gives a performer a few sharp scenes with real subtext.

lead_characters.name: Elias
lead_characters.hook: Elias is the keeper of the old world, the man who refuses to sell the last meaningful thing just because the market has collapsed. He brings a quiet moral clarity to the film and briefly reframes scarcity as a question of value, not price.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a beautiful elder-character role in the tradition of a John Hurt or Ian McKellen late-career scene part: brief, humane, and memorable. It gives an actor one of the film’s clearest moral speeches and a real emotional imprint.

lead_characters.name: Mrs. Gable
lead_characters.hook: Mrs. Gable is a comic pressure valve with teeth, the kind of old-world resident who refuses to let apocalypse erase her standards. She’s small but vivid, and her outburst helps keep the hotel from becoming too solemn.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a fun, scene-stealing elder role in the lane of June Squibb or Margo Martindale: blunt, funny, and instantly memorable. It gives an actor a sharp comic beat inside a serious film.

One older female role with a strong comic beat (Mrs. Gable)
Supporting roles skew 30s-70s and can be cast with character actors

Limited city-collapse dressing and crowd control

technical.vfx_details: Asteroid imagery, city-wide atmospheric collapse, dream/vision inserts, and impact-night environmental effects; mostly selective rather than constant.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunshots, shattering glass, practical riot dressing, body handling, and collapse aftermath.

rights_flags.detail: The Blue Note is a real venue name referenced in Morgan’s backstory.
NATO is repeatedly named as the bunker/passport authority in the premise.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: prestige theatrical platform play or streamer prestige original

budget.note: Contemporary hotel interiors keep the footprint contained, but Lisbon street collapse dressing, night exteriors, crowd scenes, and asteroid/impact visuals will push this above a bare chamber-piece.

casting.note: Morgan needs a lead who can credibly play piano on camera and carry a romantic, interior, morally conflicted role; Marie also needs an actor who can sing, spar, and hold the film’s emotional center.

development.note: The script’s emotional architecture is strong, but the George/Morgan bargain, the Marie romance, and the apocalyptic premise all need to stay in balance so the movie doesn’t feel like it’s switching genres midstream.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who respond to elevated genre, doomed romance, and prestige character pieces with a strong visual identity.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly female-skewing, urban/coastal, streamer-savvy, art-house and prestige-drama audience

budget_tier.note: One primary hotel world, a handful of Lisbon exteriors, moderate VFX, and a cast built for character actors keep this in indie feature territory.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where mood, performance, and a high-concept premise can coexist without needing tentpole scale. The script is especially attractive to buyers who want a visually distinctive, actor-forward feature with a clear emotional hook.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed emotional arc and no clear sequel or spinoff vector.

strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the movie in one sentence, which makes it easy to position as a prestige genre play rather than a hard-sell art film. That clarity helps both streamer acquisition and actor attachment because the role and the stakes are obvious immediately.
strengths.evidence: The opening establishes the asteroid countdown, the bunker passport economy, and Morgan’s need to finish the song for George.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Morgan is a real star part.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead role gives a performer a full emotional and technical showcase: piano playing, romantic tension, self-loathing, and a late moral reversal. That is exactly the kind of part that can attract a serious actor looking for a prestige reset.
strengths.evidence: Morgan’s scenes at the piano, his bargaining with George, and his final choice to walk away from the car all define a strong arc.

strengths.what_it_means: The bar, corridor, suite, and rooftop create a contained production environment that still feels rich and cinematic. That gives producers a way to sell scale without paying for true scale, which is a strong indie advantage.
strengths.evidence: Most of the story lives in the hotel complex, with only selective Lisbon exteriors and a few specialty locations.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The music concept is the film’s moat.
strengths.what_it_means: Making the song itself the object of the bargain gives the movie a built-in emotional and marketing device that is more ownable than a generic survival plot. Buyers can sell the movie on the idea that art becomes the currency of the end of the world.
strengths.evidence: George wants the finished song, Marie hears it as hope, and the final performance turns the room into a communal release.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Marie gives the movie its heart.
strengths.what_it_means: The romance is not decorative; it changes the moral math of the story and gives the film a second emotional engine beyond the bunker deal. That broadens the appeal to audiences who want feeling with their genre and gives the film a more memorable ending.
strengths.evidence: Marie challenges Morgan’s bargain, sings his song, and ultimately reframes survival as something that must still mean something.

strengths.what_it_means: The villain is not a brute; he’s a collector, which makes the conflict feel sophisticated and adult. That kind of antagonist is attractive to actors and helps the movie play in a higher-end lane.
strengths.evidence: George’s bunker photos, his calm bargaining, and his ownership language around Morgan’s music define him as a predator of taste and access.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige, actor-forward apocalypse feature with a clean hook, a contained production footprint, and a signature emotional engine built around music, survival, and moral compromise. The script’s strongest commercial asset is that it feels expensive in mood without requiring expensive scale, which makes it a credible buy for streamer originals, specialty theatrical, or prestige indie financing.

items.area: The middle repeats the same bargain pressure.
items.detail: A lot of the second act cycles through variations of Morgan being asked to play, George tightening the terms, and Marie testing his values. That keeps the atmosphere strong, but it also means the buying conversation will include whether the movie has enough escalation beyond the emotional mood and the bunker deal.

items.area: The asteroid is more mood than event.
items.detail: The apocalypse is vivid as a pressure system, but the script largely keeps the impact offscreen until the end. That choice supports the tone, but it also narrows the audience promise for buyers who want a more visible catastrophe payoff from the premise.

items.area: Morgan’s emotional turn is heavily internal.
items.detail: The lead’s final rejection of George is satisfying, but much of the shift happens through reflection, memory, and dialogue rather than external action. That makes the role rich for an actor, but it also means the film depends on performance precision more than the packaging might suggest.

She becomes increasingly central, but for a long stretch she functions as the emotional counterweight to Morgan rather than an independent driver of plot. Buyers will notice that the film’s romantic power is strong, while the female lead’s structural leverage is more conditional than her presence on the page first suggests.

items.area: The rights scan is not entirely clean.
items.detail: The script names The Blue Note and NATO, which are manageable but still require a legal pass in packaging and clearance conversations. Neither is a deal-breaker, but they are real items a buyer’s business affairs team will flag before greenlight.

issues.headline: The script’s main friction is structural, not conceptual: the hook is strong, but the middle leans hard on repeated bargaining and interior mood rather than fresh turns. Buyers will also clock that the apocalypse is mostly atmospheric until the end, which makes this a prestige play more than a catastrophe spectacle.
